passage:
Last summer my cousin Sahil kept saying, "Parveen, you're too sensitive," every time I got upset: when he laughed at my drawing, when he popped my balloon. After a while I stopped showing anything. I'd smile, then go and cry in the store room. Ammi found me there one afternoon. She didn't say I was too much. She said, "Of course that hurt. It would hurt me too." Then she taught me something: squeeze my fists hard, count to five, let go, and then say one sentence, like "That wasn't kind." The next time Sahil laughed, I tried it. My voice shook, but I said it. He actually stopped. I don't hide in the store room anymore.
Parveen

qa.q: Where did Parveen go to cry?
qa.a: Parveen went to cry in the store room.

qa.q: Why did Parveen stop showing feelings in front of Sahil?
qa.a: Being called too sensitive hurt, so Parveen began hiding feelings to avoid more remarks.

qa.q: What coping tool did Ammi teach, and how did it work?
qa.a: Squeeze fists, count to five, let go, then say one sentence; Parveen said "That wasn't kind" and Sahil stopped.

qa.q: How might Sahil have seen Parveen's feelings before that day?
qa.a: He seemed to treat them as a joke, not realising his remarks pushed Parveen into hiding.

grounding: A child called too sensitive starts hiding feelings, and a mother who says the hurt makes sense and teaches a coping tool restores confidence.

passage:
Note for Hemant's parents, from Shreya, class teacher
This week some classmates told Hemant "you're too sensitive" after he got teary during a noisy game of dodgeball. Since then I've noticed a change. He no longer tells me when something bothers him; he goes very quiet and pulls his sleeves over his hands. Yesterday I asked him privately. He said, "I'm trying not to be a baby." I told him his feelings make sense and that feeling things strongly is not babyish. We practised two tools: three slow breaths by the window, and a small card that says "I need a minute" for when it gets too loud. He used the card today. Please tell him the same at home: his feelings are welcome.

qa.q: What does Hemant do with his sleeves when something bothers him?
qa.a: He pulls his sleeves over his hands.

qa.q: What does Hemant's "I'm trying not to be a baby" show about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels ashamed of his feelings after being called too sensitive, and is trying to hide them.

qa.q: Which two tools did Shreya practise with Hemant?
qa.a: Three slow breaths by the window, and a card that says "I need a minute".

qa.q: How might Hemant's classmates see him if they watched him use the card calmly?
qa.a: They may understand he just needs a minute, not that he is a baby, which could make teasing less likely.

grounding: A teacher notices a boy hiding his feelings after being called too sensitive, tells him they make sense and teaches coping tools.

passage:
Monday. Cousin Ira laughed at Dilnaz's drawing of a horse. 'It looks like a dog!' Dilnaz's eyes filled. 'Arre, you're too sensitive,' said Chachu, and everyone laughed.
Wednesday. At school two girls told Dilnaz she couldn't sit with them. She went to the washroom, washed her face, came back smiling, and told no one.
Saturday. Ammi found her drawing in the dim room, pressing hard with the pencil. 'Something's heavy.' Dilnaz shrugged. 'I'm too sensitive.' Ammi sat down. 'Your feelings make sense. Monday hurt. Feeling things fully isn't wrong.' She showed her how to breathe out slowly and draw the feeling as a colour. Dilnaz drew a grey cloud. Then she told Ammi about Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Ira say about the horse drawing?
qa.a: 'It looks like a dog!'

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz come back from the washroom smiling and tell no one?
qa.a: After being called too sensitive, she felt ashamed of her hurt and had started hiding it.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that rebuilt Dilnaz's trust?
qa.a: She said the feelings made sense and taught slow breathing and drawing the feeling, so Dilnaz felt safe to tell her about Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Chachu have seen his remark?
qa.a: Chachu probably meant it as a light joke, not noticing how it taught Dilnaz to hide her feelings.

grounding: Shows a sensitive child who starts hiding hurt after being called too sensitive, and a parent who validates her feelings and teaches coping tools.

passage: Himani, when your Papa called you too sensitive yesterday, I saw your face close like a door. When your Jyoti Nani was ten, in Jabalpur, I cried at everything: a dead kitten, a sad song, a scolding meant for my brother. My father would say, 'Too sensitive. Stop it.' So I stopped, on the outside. I cried only in the cowshed, where no one looked. Then our new teacher, Mrs. Joseph, found me there after a bad day. She didn't laugh. She said, 'Of course it hurt. Your feelings make sense.' She gave me a small notebook. 'When it's big, write it here, breathe out slowly, and come and find me if you want.' I filled nine notebooks, Himani. And I went back to showing my face.

qa.q: Where did young Jyoti go to cry?
qa.a: To the cowshed.

qa.q: How did young Jyoti feel when her father said 'Too sensitive. Stop it'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, so she hid her feelings on the outside.

qa.q: What choice by Mrs. Joseph changed things for Jyoti?
qa.a: Finding her in the cowshed, saying her feelings made sense, and giving her a notebook and slow breathing to cope.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Joseph have felt finding Jyoti in the cowshed?
qa.a: Mrs. Joseph was probably concerned and tender, seeing a child hiding her tears alone.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a sensitive child who hid her feelings after being called too sensitive, until a teacher validated them and taught coping tools.

passage: Dadi's birthday guests were due in twenty minutes, the pooja was half set up, and Ishita was sobbing on the bedroom floor. The new lehenga scratched her waist like sandpaper. 'Honestly, Sangeeta, she's too sensitive,' Bua called from the hall. Ishita pressed her face into her knees so nobody could see. Sangeeta had a hundred things to do. She knelt anyway. 'It really does itch. That's not silly.' She fetched the soft cotton slip and slid it underneath. 'Now three slow breaths with me. Then sit in here till you're ready.' Ishita breathed. The doorbell rang. Ten minutes later she came out on her own, and when Bua started to say something, Sangeeta said, 'She's fine. She knows her own skin.'

qa.q: What did Sangeeta slide under the lehenga?
qa.a: The soft cotton slip.

qa.q: Why did Ishita press her face into her knees?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed after Bua's remark and wanted to hide her feelings.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do, even under time pressure, that protected Ishita's trust?
qa.a: She knelt, agreed the itch was real, fixed it with the slip, taught three slow breaths and let Ishita choose when to come out.

qa.q: How might Bua see Ishita after Sangeeta's reply?
qa.a: Bua may begin to see Ishita's reaction as knowing her own skin rather than fussing.

grounding: Shows a sensitive child hurt by being called too sensitive, and a parent who, even in a rush, says the feeling makes sense and teaches a coping tool.

passage:
Vasudha cried when her drawing tore in the lift of their Pune building. Her uncle laughed. "Arre, so sensitive! It's just paper."
After that, she started swallowing things. When her friend left her out at the park, she said, "It's fine." When a cartoon made her sad, she went to the bathroom to cry.
Her father, Shankar, noticed the red eyes. That night he sat on her bed. "You've gone very quiet lately."
"Chacha says I'm too sensitive."
Shankar was quiet for a moment. "Your feelings make sense to me. Being left out hurts. So does a torn drawing you worked hard on." He handed her a small cushion. "When it's big, squeeze this and tell me one word for it."
Vasudha squeezed. "Sad."
"Good word," he said.

qa.q: What did Vasudha's uncle say when she cried about the drawing?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "Arre, so sensitive! It's just paper."

qa.q: Why did Vasudha start hiding her feelings?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed after being called too sensitive, so she said "It's fine" and cried alone in the bathroom.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that could rebuild Vasudha's trust?
qa.a: He told her the feelings made sense and gave her a coping tool: squeeze the cushion and name the feeling in one word.

qa.q: What would change if Shankar had also said she was too sensitive?
qa.a: Vasudha would likely keep hiding her feelings and stop coming to him, feeling there was no safe person to tell.

grounding: Shows a sensitive child hurt by being called too sensitive and a father who validates her feelings while teaching a simple coping tool.
